explanation: Recognise an extension of the collection and the need to separate attention, access and learning.
evidence: Thirteen animals received digital stories, and when a visitor pointed a device at a specimen, the app could place flesh, movement, or internal mechanisms over the bones.

The designers intended an extension of the collection rather than a replacement for it, and the curatorial project examined whether augmented reality could connect old objects with an interpretive and interactive layer of digital visualisation.
A three-dimensional model could be superimposed over a skeleton while tracking adjusted its orientation and size as the visitor moved, helping explain functional anatomy.

The device recorded selected content and viewing duration, while researchers noted stops and behaviour before inviting visitors to complete a questionnaire or interview, gathering 199 questionnaires and 15 interviews over the 92 days of the study in 2015.
The combination allowed them to compare what people did with accounts of their experience.
A brief stop is insufficient evidence of learning, while the physical specimens are irreplaceable for comparing the screen with the shapes on display.
This distinction matters because technical interruption can affect measured engagement independently of interest or comprehension.

Interpretation requires care when researchers observe numerous visitors using the app to inspect specimens, because an apparently engaging experience might reflect the novelty of an immersive display, or a chance to manipulate a virtual feature, instead of attention to the actual skeleton.
Crowds, competing sound and inconsistent connectivity can also affect participation.
To conclude that the application is an effective learning aid, an advocate would need evidence of what people could explain afterward.
A follow-up question could suggest whether an animated projection helped a visitor identify the movement of a particular joint.
